records.name: Oaxaca
records.summary:
In May 2024 the organising brotherhood of a flagship traditional festival in this region circulated a written invitation stating that "men dressed as women will not be admitted"; muxe activists filed a discrimination complaint with the national equality body. These festivals are explicitly marketed to foreign tourists - the exclusion is directly visitor-facing.

April 2025 reporting profiles the region as the country's fastest-growing tourist paradise and at the same time its most dangerous state for the LGBT+ community: several violent incidents are under investigation with possible municipal-police participation, in municipalities where armed groups operate, and the state's answer has been stepped-up visitor security rather than institutional reform. The state human-rights ombudsperson opened 34 discrimination investigations involving LGBTIQ+ people between 2015 and 2022, and violence against muxes persists despite the state's international reputation for diversity.

The legal layer points the other way: the state has allowed legal gender recognition since 2019, extended it to age 12 and above by decree in 2021, and a 2023 Supreme Court ruling fully opened the procedure. The result is coexistence: a formally protective legal framework alongside customary exclusion enforced at the exact events tourists attend.

records.name: Puebla
records.summary:
Puebla led the national statistics for 2025 with 7 recorded killings of LGBT+ people; trans women constituted 58.3% of all such killings nationwide that year, across at least 17 states reporting victims. Its legal-gender-recognition law (2021) keeps an 18-year minimum-age requirement that the Supreme Court voided in March 2022, yet the state congress has still not corrected the text — legislative non-compliance with a final court ruling is itself a hostility signal directly relevant to a visitor whose documents must match presentation. There is no dedicated investigative machinery, no transfeminicide offence, and no state-level enforcement data.

The combination of top-of-table lethality and open defiance of the judiciary distinguishes Puebla from states that simply lack statutes: here a statute exists but the legislature actively refuses to conform it to a binding ruling. Context for comparison: Mexico City, which also had high counts in 2024-25, created a transfeminicide investigation unit and mandatory-response protocol within months; Estado de México, which likewise defies a Supreme Court ruling on recognition, has at least had a penal-code hate-crime provision covering bias motives since 2021. Puebla has neither the court-compliant text nor any criminal-law protection or enforcement innovation.

records.name: Tripura
records.summary:
This state shows the country's clearest pattern of border-checkpoint profiling of gender-nonconforming presentation. In August 2024 police reported apprehending 15 Bangladeshi nationals including seven transgender people in separate incidents within 24 hours, one group seized at a highway check post en route to India's financial capital, some described by police as "disguised as third-gender" - the explicit frame that trans presentation is a cover for infiltration. A coordinated November 2024 sweep detained twelve more, including minors and transgender people. The state shares a long, porous international border, which sustains the checkpoint geography. These are named-state-actor operations with published counts, directly facing any trans-presenting visitor crossing by land.

The institutional counterweight is nominal: the state is one of only twelve states/UTs to have constituted a transgender welfare board under national rules, but a right-to-information investigation found most such boards leaderless or inactive, with no compliance mechanism and no real power. On the audited record there is no statute criminalising trans presence here; the documented harm is police practice at the checkpoints.

records.name: West Bengal
records.summary:
West Bengal replicates the Tripura checkpoint script: South Dinajpur police arrested a Bangladeshi transgender person for allegedly "infiltrating India," treating trans presentation as evidence of illegal entry rather than identity; police also detained the e-rickshaw driver who carried her from the border. The state shares a long Bangladesh border and falls within the same policing logic. West Bengal is also one of only three states recording cases under the Transgender Persons Act in 2021 (3 of 7 nationally), indicating some legal infrastructure exists but also that trans-targeted crime is occurring at a detectable rate.

Against the national 0.43, West Bengal sits −0.09. The border profiling is visitor-facing and state-actor-driven, but the incidents are fewer and less concentrated than Tripura's repeated-sweep pattern. Compared to Tripura (0.31), West Bengal's harm is a single documented arrest plus the broader infiltration framing rather than repeated mass operations; compared to Delhi (0.38), which shares the profiling language but also has India's strongest institutional trans presence, West Bengal lacks that offsetting civic infrastructure outside Kolkata.

A welfare board exists (one of 12 states/UTs with a constituted body), but per the RTI investigation it operates without a functioning policy framework. For a foreign visitor transiting the land border, the primary exposure is the same appearance-as-suspicion-trigger mechanism documented in Tripura.

records.name: Punjab
records.summary:
In Amritsar — the spiritual centre of the region's dominant faith — Pride Amritsar cancelled its 27 April 2025 parade at the Rose Garden after "mounting resistance" from Sikh religious organisations, including the Nihang Singh faction and the Akal Takht, the faith's highest temporal authority; organisers cited religious-group opposition as the reason for cancelling the annual event (Washington Blade, 23 April 2025). No other Punjab-specific law, ordinance or institution affecting trans people appears in the audited sources for this record.

For a trans visitor the documented signal is institutional, not criminal: no statute here targets trans people, but an organised religious authority compelled the cancellation of the region's annual public trans assembly, and the event simply did not happen. Public visibility in Amritsar therefore carries a documented precedent of organised religious opposition, and the absence of any recorded state intervention to preserve the event is part of that record.

records.name: Tamil Nādu
records.summary:
Tamil Nadu is India's most protective sub-national regime for trans visitors. It was the first state to introduce a transgender welfare policy (1995), maintains a dedicated Transgender Welfare Board (as the Third Gender Welfare Board since 15 April 2008) within the Social Welfare & Women Empowerment Department, and adopted a comprehensive State Policy for Transgender Persons in 2025. On 4 August 2025, the Madras High Court (WP 7284 of 2021) expressly commended the policy as "a victory for transgender and intersex persons after their long struggle" — active judicial confirmation of executive protection is rare and meaningful for a visitor's institutional recourse. Tamil Nadu was the only state recording a Transgender Persons Act case in 2020 (1 of 1 nationally) and logged 7 of the 11 national cases in 2023 — its courts are demonstrably being used.

Against the national 0.43, Tamil Nadu sits +0.10. The state has a functioning (by comparison) policy apparatus, court validation, and the Thirunangai/Thirunambi administrative categories embedded in governance. Compared to Kerala (0.50), Tamil Nadu adds the explicit court commendation and longer institutional history; compared to Punjab (0.35), which saw a religious authority veto trans public assembly, Tamil Nadu's state machinery actively protects it. A complicating signal exists — Hindu transgender devotees in Madurai announced a fast in December 2025 over temple lamp-lighting decisions — but this reflects trans people as political actors in state governance, not state suppression of them.

records.name: Kerala
records.summary:
Kerala holds a constituted Transgender Welfare Board — one of the 12 states/UTs reported to the federal parliament in December 2021 as having set one up under the national trans-protection rules (PIB) — and its law-enforcement machinery is measurably engaged: the state registered 2 of the 7 national cases under the Transgender Persons Act in 2021 and 4 of the 11 recorded in 2023, among the highest sub-national totals in those years (queerbeat data report, 30 January 2026).

That activity should be read with the source's own caveat: national recording is sparse (20 cases across 2019–23) because of police registration bias, against survey data showing 27.2% physical and 22.3% sexual violence prevalence (2025 Transgender Health study, n=4,964). Registered cases therefore evidence a system that at least accepts complaints, not rarity of violence. No Kerala-specific restriction is documented; for a visitor the picture is one of institutional recognition machinery in a state where such machinery exists and is used.

records.name: Assam
records.summary:
Assam appears in national crime records with 2 of the 7 cases registered under the Transgender Persons Act in 2021, and none in the 2023 tally (queerbeat data report, 30 January 2026) — which itself cautions that national counts are tiny (20 cases 2019–23) because of police registration bias, with 2025 survey data showing 27.2% physical and 22.3% sexual violence prevalence. Recorded cases prove the complaint system is reachable, not that violence is uncommon.

In the December 2021 federal reply listing the 12 states/UTs that had constituted Transgender Welfare Boards (PIB), Assam is not among them — i.e., no state welfare machinery stood in place as of that date. No Assam-specific protective or restrictive statute, ordinance or checkpoint operation is documented in the audited sources; the record supports a thin official-visibility finding balanced against the region-wide caveats, nothing more.
